cultivar: Fenghuang Shui Xian, Jiang Hua Xiang strain
processing: Sun-withered, shaken firmly overnight to a medium oxidation that brings out its spicy aroma, fixed, rolled into long strips and charcoal roasted to a medium level.
harvest_season: Spring, late April into May; a mid-to-late strain picked once, with the high-mountain lots coming in last.
appearance_dry: Long, tightly twisted dark brown strips with a spicy-sweet smell.
appearance_wet: Long, thick olive leaves with pronounced red edges.
taste_profile: A spicy floral aroma like ginger lily and white ginger blossom, honey and ripe fruit behind it, a medium-full body with a warming, faintly peppery tingle and a long, cooling, sweet finish.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps. The ginger-flower note is strongest on the lid and in the aftertaste; let the cup cool slightly before sipping and it shows better.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually from autumn after a medium roast and a rest; the spicy character settles with a few months and lots from the previous year are common and often better. Keeps two to four years sealed and dry.
description:
Jiang Hua Xiang, ginger flower fragrance, is the spicy one among the Phoenix dancong aroma types: not the heat of ginger root but the scent of the ginger lily, a white garden flower with a sweet, slightly peppery perfume, carried on a medium-full oolong from the Fenghuang Mountains above Chaozhou.

It is one of the ten classic types and has a famous ancestor. The mother tree, called Tong Tian Xiang, fragrance reaching heaven, stands in Zhong Ping on Wudong and is said to be several centuries old; tea from that tree and its direct cuttings is sold under the Tong Tian Xiang name, while Jiang Hua Xiang is the aroma type in general, grown from cuttings across the range. The two are the same strain at different distances from the original tree.

The spice comes from the plant and from firm shaking during the overnight oxidation stage, which makers push a little further than for the delicate floral strains; the leaf is then rolled into strips and given a medium charcoal roast that knits the spice into honey. In the cup the aroma is ginger lily and white flowers, the taste is honeyed with ripe fruit, there is a faint warming tingle on the tongue and the finish is long, cool and sweet.

Brew it with the usual dancong technique, plenty of leaf, boiling water, instant pours, and let the cup cool for a moment before drinking: the ginger-flower note shows more clearly just below scalding. It lasts eight steeps and holds its character to the end.

It is sold by year, mostly from autumn, and a few months of rest after roasting does it good, so a lot from last spring is a fair buy. Prices rise steeply as you approach Wudong and the named tree; honest high-mountain Jiang Hua Xiang is the sensible place to start, and Tong Tian Xiang is the splurge once you know you like the style.
sources_note: The identification of Tong Tian Xiang as the Jiang Hua Xiang mother tree in Zhong Ping, Wudong, follows Chaozhou tea sources; the tree's age (often given as 400 years or more) is traditional.
